mfrmr roadmap

Source: ROADMAP.md

mfrmr connects three tasks in performance assessment:

  1. Measurement models: estimate person ability while accounting for rater severity, task or criterion difficulty, category thresholds, and supported discrimination or dependence structures.
  2. G-theory assessment planning: separate observed-score variance components in a G-Study and project reliability, generalizability (G), dependability (Phi), and standard errors across candidate rating designs in a D-Study.
  3. Rater feedback and decision support: turn agreement, fit, residual, network, bias/DFF, and conditional classification analyses into structured, reviewable evidence without automating high-stakes rater exclusion or causal fairness claims.

This document outlines the planned capability sequence across 0.3.0, 0.3.x, and 0.4.x, together with the statistical and software boundaries that govern each stage. For changes already implemented in the current development tree (0.2.4.9000), see NEWS and the help("mfrmr_api_migration_030").

Starting from the published 0.2.4 release

CRAN published 0.2.4 on 2026-10-30. It is the stable reference for this roadmap; 0.2.4.9000 is development toward 0.3.0, not a replacement already available from CRAN.

Area Published 0.2.4 Intended change in 0.3.0
Public entry points 189 exports 163 exports: consolidate 28 names into shared routes and add facets_guide() / import_irt_fit(). Follow the migration guide for exact replacements.
Two-family GPCM Experimental two-facet MML Choose two slope facets among fixed additive facets, with separate step ownership and a named slope reference; retain experimental inference limits.
Model specification Flat fit_mfrm() arguments Group advanced model choices in spec and numerical settings in control, with validated legacy calls.
Figures and saved results Existing S3 routes and legacy plot payloads Return ggplot objects consistently; use plot_data() for numerical payloads. Preserve saved-result classes and supported methods.
Bayesian workflows Export and posterior-summary review Direct data/spec export, optional CmdStanR execution, joint-draw contrasts and new-Person scoring with separate predictive-precision checks.
Assessment planning G-Study / D-Study and paired contrasts Review a declared finite set of plans against costs, limits and targets, preserving pointwise uncertainty and avoiding an automatic optimum claim.
Learning and reference Extensive reference help and tutorials A visual entry page, five core offline tutorials, specialist website articles and shorter task-focused reference navigation.

Reliability plots and compute_information() already exist in 0.2.4; they are not new statistical capabilities in 0.3.0. Improve their visibility and interpretation: distinguish Person/rater separation, observed agreement, G/Phi and ability-dependent information. The current information total uses all observed rating exposures; it must not be presented as an individual person’s test information or EAP uncertainty. A future explicit rating-roster interface requires its own design specification and numerical validation.

The release remains conditional on cross-platform checks and acceptable check duration. An implemented feature or a successful local check alone does not establish release readiness.

What should become easier in 0.3.0?

The intended benefit is a connected assessment workflow: start with a rating table, understand the design and diagnostics, and use the results to prepare feedback or compare a future rating plan. The interactive tour shows this sequence with data, figures, explanations and a saved analysis.

Your question The workflow should help you do this
Can I compare people rated by different panels? Inspect who rated whom, distinguish missing assignments from zero scores, and review model identification. A connected graph alone is insufficient.
What should I discuss with a rater? Read severity together with consistency, exposure and uncertainty; prepare a reviewable report without automatic rater exclusion.
Should I add raters or tasks? Compare declared plans using G/Phi, uncertainty and resource constraints. A D-Study is a separate observed-score analysis, not a transformation of an MFRM coefficient.
Can I reproduce this result later? Save the analysis, diagnostics and numerical plot data together, and reload them for reporting.

TAM or FACETS can remain the right choice for a particular model or established workflow. mfrmr’s aim is to reduce the work between analysis and an interpretable assessment decision. More model options alone would not achieve that aim; beginner comprehension and successful use still need evaluation.

0.3.0: migration and release conditions

The capabilities in the comparison table are implemented in the development source. They are not yet a CRAN release. The next release is 0.3.0 because consolidating public names and changing plot() returns require script updates:

  • Replace retired entry points using the help("mfrmr_api_migration_030").
  • Extract plotted numerical values with plot_data(); plot() returns a ggplot object. Supported saved 0.2.x result classes and legacy plot payloads retain their documented methods.
  • Use complete argument names with fit_mfrm() and do.call(). Only the first four positional arguments retain their old positions. Abbreviations for names now passed through ... are not supported; the migration guide gives before/after calls.

Interface changes and faster numerical kernels retain the documented statistical targets, quadrature rules, convergence criteria and independent checks. They do not establish finite-sample inference validity for additional models or rating designs. Shared spec lists remain subject to each function’s scope, including the export limits below.

Remaining release work is to resolve cross-platform check failures and duration, verify saved-object and reporting workflows against the final archive, and publish documentation that matches the released source. A successful local check or completed implementation does not close these conditions. Version milestones express dependencies and evidence requirements, not calendar dates.

Alternative response equations and later model candidates below are outside 0.3.0. Errors or misleading claims within its supported scope still require correction. Later extensions are selected for a concrete assessment decision and the evidence needed to support it; they are not a commitment to implement every branch.

Measurement models: current limits and extension order

Model choice and estimation method are separate decisions. Current native support in 0.2.4.9000 is bounded as follows; consult help("mfrmr_gpcm_scope") and help("fit_mfrm_technical_details") for the complete conditions.

Response model Native estimation paths Boundary that extensions must preserve
Ordinary RSM / PCM MML, ordinary JML and CML within their documented scopes; a separate Jeffreys-penalized JML path Fixed versus estimated ability populations change the MML model. Numerical admissibility alone does not validate small-sample intervals.
One-family GPCM, shared step and slope facet MML, ordinary JML and experimental profile-score-adjusted JML The adjustment is not a general small-sample correction for every model; its root-variation SE does not establish structural-parameter interval coverage.
One-family GPCM, separate step and slope facets MML JML and its profile-score adjustment are not supported for this specification.
Two-family GPCM Experimental fixed-grid EM or adaptive-direct MML Two named slope facets among the declared fixed additive facets; step ownership, the noncentered location facet and the geometric-mean-one slope reference are separately specified. Ability remains fixed to N(0,1).

The development implementation retains the current response equation, in which both slope factors multiply the whole ability-minus-location-and-step expression. For example, Task and Rater can own slopes while Criterion owns steps. Use slope_reference to name the slope family with geometric mean one and noncenter_facet to name the sole uncentered location facet. Additional Occasion or Venue effects remain fixed additive effects, not extra ability dimensions. The old two-facet defaults and saved fits retain their meaning. Extended portable calibrations use format 7; the original two-facet structure retains format 6.

Three- and five-facet calculations and representative workflows are checked. These checks do not guarantee identification, convergence or interval coverage for every design. In particular, an optimizer can converge while the integration checks refuse intervals or portable scoring. Extended-role Stan export from an existing fit supports posterior reload, contrasts, plots and reports. Two-family simulation, direct data/spec export and new-Person posterior scoring remain unsupported. Changing the slope reference with fresh independent priors changes the Bayesian model. This extension is included in 0.3.0. Its point-estimation review separates identification, numerical accuracy and sampling error; adding support does not remove experimental interval restrictions.

A bounded three-facet study now separates Person count from ratings per Person. All numerical checks passed, but the 60-Person, four-rating Task-slope interval covered its true value in 183/200 replications. The design, Monte Carlo uncertainty and precision results are described in the development GPCM guide. They do not establish a general minimum sample size or remove experimental interval restrictions. The number of levels of each facet was fixed at two.

The 0.3.0 review distinguishes reliable computation from inferential recommendations:

  1. Specify the model and supported designs. Keep the response equation, category support, population, location constraints and slope normalization explicit. Changing a reference must preserve probabilities; changing the step owner generally changes the model. Identify confounded or insufficient rating designs before promising estimation.
  2. Verify point estimation before recommending intervals. Check objective values and estimates under independent starting values and integration refinement; separate local curvature from existence of a finite, unique optimum. Assess bias and RMSE on each parameter’s stated scale, with Monte Carlo uncertainty, retaining failed attempts in the denominator.
  3. Complete the supported workflow. Connect estimation and numerical audits to intervals, prediction, saved-result reload, reporting and calibration export. Document and reject unsupported simulation or Bayesian-export combinations. Existing saved fits must retain their original equation and owner conventions.
  4. Evaluate the intended inference. Use independent calculations and targeted finite-sample studies for the adopted model, estimand and rating design. Successful reference calculations are not production implementation, and new computational support does not remove experimental interval limits.

Two-family JML, its bias correction, alternative slope placement and the Uto (2021) response equation are separate candidates. They require their own identification and estimation contracts. A Bayesian implementation must specify the link coefficient, ability scale and constrained prior density; reproducing the published appendix and adopting a different symmetric prior are distinct choices. A logistic link with coefficient 1.7 is not an exact normal-ogive link. Metric conversion must preserve probabilities and transform covariance and priors consistently.

These candidates are considered alongside ordinary-model needs: mixed binary and polytomous category sets, rubric differences, and uncertainty in linked calibrations. Current native fits use one declared category range; a step facet does not provide facet-specific category support. The choice to extend mfrmr or use a supported TAM/ConQuest workflow depends on the required model and outputs, not a goal of reproducing every external modeling option.

Covariate interactions inside population_formula and rating-facet interactions in facet_interactions represent different statistical terms with different identification constraints; they will be specified and validated separately rather than merged. Exported Bayesian models share the measurement model’s response equation and add explicit priors; their posterior summaries and credible intervals are not native MML point estimates, Wald intervals, or likelihood-ratio tests. See help("export_mfrm_model"), help("read_mfrm_posterior"), and help("predict.mfrm_posterior_summary").

Assessment planning, rater assignment, and feedback principles

G-theory planning and operational design comparison

Univariate and multivariate G-Study and D-Study workflows, paired multivariate D-study comparisons, and design simulations remain first-class capabilities that do not require Bayesian software. Classical observed-score generalizability and IRT/MFRM latent-scale precision answer complementary questions and keep distinct labels, variance denominators, and interval assumptions. Beyond the finite feasible plan comparison in 0.3.0, broader sparse future rosters, adaptive rater allocation, and post-selection plan adjustments remain separate research-backed extensions so single-plan intervals are never overstated as optimal-design guarantees. See help("mfrmr_methods_reference"), help("mfrmr_workflow_methods"), and the vignette("mfrmr-gtheory", package = "mfrmr").

Rater assignment, linking, and anchors

Guidance and diagnostics for complete and incomplete rating networks distinguish direct parameter anchors, group-mean anchors, and unanchored common-person/common-rater linking. No single percentage of common ratings guarantees a stable common scale across designs: graph connectivity, overlap geometry, anchor fit, and empirical drift all matter. Fixed anchors impose exact scale constraints and do not by themselves establish invariance or propagate prior calibration uncertainty; cohort shifts, panel-wide severity shifts, and individual rater drift require identifiable comparisons (0.3.x and later). See help("fit_mfrm") and the help("mfrm_calibration_workflow").

Sample-size guidance must distinguish Persons, raters, tasks, common recordings and ratings per Person, and name the target: ability, severity contrast, cohort difference or population variance. Existing evidence does not establish one minimum sample size for all RSM/PCM uses. Further interval work must distinguish variance-boundary behavior, population misspecification and prior-calibration uncertainty; adding observations cannot resolve a confounded rubric or recording mode. Compare coverage, interval width and unavailable results together before recommending a correction or resampling method.

Rater feedback and diagnostic screening

Severity estimates, infit/outfit MnSq and ZSTD, centrality/restriction indices, exact and weighted agreement, bias/DFF screens, residual networks, and exploratory clustering help assessment teams decide which ratings, criteria, or raters warrant substantive review. They are not automatic judgments of test fairness, rater competence, or training causal effects. Future feedback improvements prioritize clearer diagnostic explanations and cohesive mfrm_results() / mfrm_report() synthesis. Evaluate whether intended users can interpret these outputs; working examples and readable figures alone do not establish that outcome.

0.4.x and later model branches

New model families will be introduced only when their identification rules, independent numerical reference checks, inferential properties, and practical reporting workflow are established for a concrete assessment question.

Target series Intended capability Initial scope and methodological boundary
0.4.x: Multidimensional rubric profiles Low-dimensional domain profiles, domain correlations, joint profile contrasts, and criterion/rater feedback Start with a prespecified simple between-item binary loading matrix QQ on one rubric facet and unit slopes. Evaluate native MML initially for D∈{2,3}D \in \{2, 3\} and Stan HMC for explicitly supported dimensions, with measured accuracy and resource limits. Verify reduction to the corresponding unit-slope model with matching step, link and scale conventions. Define and validate subscore added value for the intended score before recommending domain reporting.
0.4.x+: Rating-process and response/scoring time models Joint or linked review of rating outcomes with timing observations Model person production/response time and rater scoring time as distinct observation processes; never duplicate one event duration across multiple criterion rows as independent likelihood contributions.
0.4.x+: Direct rater-effect and latent-class extensions Bounded parametric centrality, halo, or restricted rater-class models for targeted operational questions Establish label-switching/scale identification and compare against simpler additive + diagnostic workflows under sparse designs before public adoption.
0.4.x+: Attribute-based cognitive diagnosis Bounded rater-effects cognitive-diagnosis workflow with an explicit discrete skill-QQ matrix Restrict initial support to small, prespecified binary attribute profiles; keep discrete skill-QQ cognitive diagnosis strictly separate in parameterization and interface from continuous multidimensional loading-QQ MFRM and exploratory clustering.

The initial simple-loading model is not a reproduction of Uto (2021)’s freely varying positive loadings. General cross-loadings require explicit axis and rotation constraints; a prior that selects an orientation is not likelihood identification. Nor does setting one dimension make Uto (2021)’s equation identical to the current Uto & Ueno (2020) type two-family equation. These distinctions must be resolved before implementation or performance studies.

Foundational references for these extensions include Uto & Ueno (2020), Uto (2021), Haberman (2008), Shan & Wang (2020), and Ulitzsch et al. (2023). Haberman’s PRMSE framework motivates the subscore question; its applicability and estimator must be specified for the chosen score target. Better global fit alone does not establish useful subscores. Because these model classes exist in the psychometric literature, mfrmr evaluates contributions by transparency of assumptions, numerical reliability, and end-to-end usability rather than model-name count.

Interoperability, ergonomics, and release-readiness standards

Existing external-software routes provide a baseline; the 0.3.x work is bounded extension of those routes, not the introduction of interoperability:

Software Existing route Candidate change after 0.3.0 Acceptance boundary
FACETS Scorefile/fit-table reading, fit review and terminology guides No new general-equivalence promise; retain explicit convention differences Extreme scores, weights, anchors and fit-statistic degrees of freedom must be compared under matching conventions.
TAM; eRm and mirt Import documented fitted components on the source scale through import_irt_fit() Extend reporting for supported TAM outputs while retaining their source-model meaning DesignCell locations do not identify separate facet effects or their joint covariance without the underlying design mapping. No new generic eRm/mirt importer is planned here.
ConQuest Export bundles and normalization for demonstrated additive overlap specifications Extend comparisons for bounded polytomous additive RSM/PCM specifications Match response equations, scale constraints and uncertainty definitions; retain unsupported cases explicitly.

Do not merge MML, unpenalized JML, bias-corrected JML, CML, G-theory ANOVA/MLS, and Bayesian HMC outputs merely because they produce similarly shaped tables. See the help("mfrmr_gpcm_scope"), help("build_conquest_overlap_bundle"), and help("import_irt_fit").

mfrmr separates four distinct readiness layers rather than treating implementation completion as universal inferential validity:

  1. API and reference-oracle integration: the response equation, scale/sign orientation, and identification constraints are enforced before computation; point estimates, derivatives/intervals, and fail-closed rejections agree with an independent reference calculation; and all public entry points are covered by behavioral regression tests.
  2. Saved-object compatibility and external-software boundaries: archived 0.2.x RDS results reload cleanly across R sessions, checksum/basis provenance is verified, and structural non-equivalences with external software are stated explicitly.
  3. Runtime numerical admissibility: for a specific dataset and rating design, graph connectivity, boundary existence, positive-definite curvature, quadrature stability, or MCMC mixing gates govern whether quantities are reported as available, unavailable, or requiring review.
  4. Finite-sample inferential and decision acceptance: frequentist coverage or simulation-based calibration (counting failed or inadmissible replicates in the denominator), subscore added value, and protection against practical misinterpretation are evaluated separately from numerical convergence.
